Findings.Comment: `totalWithVat` converts the cent-denominated subtotal to euros (`subtotal(lines) / 100`), applies the VAT rate as a floating-point euro amount, then scales back up. That is arithmetic on money as floating-point euros, which the project guideline forbids: `Cents` must stay integer cents end to end. On realistic input the result is not even an integer — e.g. one line of `1999` cents at `vatRate = 0.19` yields `19.99 * 1.19 * 100 = 2378.8100000000003`, and since `as Cents` is only a type assertion it does not round, so the function returns a fractional, inexact cent value that will break equality checks, formatting, and any downstream total.
Findings.Headline: VAT total computes money in floating-point euros
Findings.Suggestion:
const cents = subtotal(lines);
  return Math.round(cents * (1 + vatRate)) as Cents;
Evidence: export function totalWithVat(lines: Line[], vatRate: number): Cents {

Expected.why: The total is computed in floating-point euros and returned unrounded as Cents, which the blocking rule forbids and which yields fractional cents.

Findings.Comment: The new `/orders/{id}/lines` endpoint queries the database directly from `OrderController` via the injected `JdbcTemplate`, bypassing `OrderService`. The project guidelines (blocking rule B1) require that controllers never access the database and that every query goes through a service; the existing `/orders/{id}` handler already follows this by delegating to `orders.find(id)`. Move this query into `OrderService` and have the controller call it.
Findings.Headline: Controller queries the database directly via JdbcTemplate
Evidence: public List<Map<String, Object>> lines(@PathVariable long id) {
return jdbc.queryForList("SELECT sku, qty FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = ?", id);

Findings.Comment: `OrderController` now holds a `JdbcTemplate` field alongside `OrderService`, so two data-access paths coexist in one controller: `/orders/{id}` goes through the service while `/orders/{id}/lines` hits the DB directly. Anyone adding another endpoint here has a live precedent for the direct path; removing the `jdbc` field and routing through `OrderService` keeps the class consistent with its own existing pattern.
Findings.Headline: Mixed data-access paths in OrderController

Expected.why: The new endpoint queries order_lines from the controller, which the blocking rule forbids. A reviewer may anchor on the query (29), the method (28) or the injected field (15).

Per the project's blocking rule, every handler that loads an invoice by id must call `authz.SameTenant(r, inv.TenantID)` before returning it. Any authenticated caller who can guess or enumerate another tenant's invoice id receives that tenant's invoice data.
Findings.Headline: Get handler returns invoice without SameTenant check

Findings.Comment: Removing the end clamp means `page` now slices `items[start : start+size]` without bounding `start+size` to `len(items)`. Any call where the final page is partial panics with an out-of-range slice: e.g. 10 items, `size = 25`, `n = 1` gives `start = 0`, which passes the `start >= len(items)` guard, then slices `items[0:25]`. The guard only rejects pages that begin past the end; it does not protect a page that extends past it.
Findings.Headline: page() slices past end of slice and panics on a partial last page

Expected.why: Without the clamp, start+size passes len(items) on a partial last page and the slice expression panics. No blocking rule covers it.

Findings.Comment: The retry condition is inverted relative to the removed `if !retryable(err)` and to the doc comment on `Deliver`, which promises transient failures are retried with exponential backoff and permanent ones returned at once. As written, `retryable` is true for every non-permanent error (network error, 5xx, 429, 408), so the very first transient failure is returned immediately and the retry loop, backoff and the "giving up after N attempts" message become unreachable; conversely a permanent error (a 4xx the endpoint will reject again) now sleeps and is re-posted five times. A single connection reset against a healthy endpoint aborts the delivery instead of retrying.
Findings.Headline: Retry condition inverted in Deliver; transient errors are never retried

Expected.why: Transient failures such as a 503 are now returned on the first attempt without any retry, while permanently rejected deliveries are retried five times with backoff.

Findings.Comment: `FetchDiff` now builds the request and reads the body with `context.Background()` instead of the caller's `ctx`, so the incoming `ctx` is ignored entirely. A caller that sets a timeout or cancels (e.g. a request handler whose HTTP context is cancelled when the client disconnects, or a job with a deadline) can no longer abort this call: the Bitbucket request and the capped body read run to completion on their own, hanging the caller past its deadline and leaking the goroutine/connection until the transport gives up. The doc comment on the function explicitly promises the opposite — "The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read" — so the code now contradicts the documented contract as well.
Findings.Headline: FetchDiff ignores caller context and cannot be cancelled or timed out
Evidence: // The caller's context bounds the whole operation, including the body read.

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: `Hold` still converts the hold duration to seconds (`int64(d.Seconds())`) while `Store.Touch` now interprets its third argument as milliseconds. Passing a realistic hold of `30s` sets the key's TTL to 30 ms, so the session is dropped long before the long-running export finishes, and `Resume` afterwards returns `ErrNotFound`. It also rejects any hold under one second, since `int64(500*time.Millisecond.Seconds())` truncates to 0 and `Touch` errors on a non-positive TTL.
Findings.Headline: Hold passes seconds to Touch which now expects milliseconds
Evidence: func (s *Store) Touch(ctx context.Context, id string, ttlMillis int64) error {

Expected.why: Touch now takes milliseconds, so a hold of two hours sets a lifetime of 7.2 seconds and the session expires while the export it was meant to cover is still running.

Findings.Comment: `Delete` reads and writes `c.items` without holding `c.mu`, while `Set` and `Get` both lock it. Two goroutines where one calls `Set` (or `Get`) and the other calls `Delete` on the same `Cache` perform concurrent map read/write, which aborts the process with `fatal error: concurrent map read and map write` in Go. Any caller that hits this cache from multiple request goroutines (the reason the mutex exists at all) can reach it as soon as `Delete` is used alongside `Set`.
Findings.Headline: Delete mutates the cache map without holding the mutex
Findings.Suggestion:
func (c *Cache) Delete(key string) bool {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	_, ok := c.items[key]
	delete(c.items, key)
	return ok
}

Expected.why: Delete touches c.items without c.mu while Set and Get hold it: a data race, and Go aborts the process on a concurrent map write.

Findings.Comment: `cancel` compares two `Long` values with `!=`, which is reference identity, not value equality. `requesterAccountId` is a boxed `Long` parameter (autoboxed at the call site) and `sourceAccountId` comes from the persisted `Transfer` record, so for account ids outside the `Long` cache range (-128..127) the two objects are distinct instances even when the ids are equal. A caller cancelling its own transfer then always gets `TransferAccessDeniedException`, while `create` on line 61 uses `sourceAccountId.equals(targetAccountId)` for the same kind of comparison.
Findings.Headline: Long identity comparison denies legit cancellations

Expected.why: Boxed Longs are compared by reference, so for any account id above 127 the owner's own cancellation is rejected as access denied.

Findings.Comment: Replacing `defer r.mu.Unlock()` with an explicit unlock at the end of `Disable` leaves the early-return path for an unknown slug returning while still holding `r.mu`. Any call such as `Disable("no-such-team", "x")` that follows a legitimate `Disable`/lookup on the same `Registry` returns the error but never releases the mutex, so every subsequent `Registry` method that locks `mu` blocks forever and the process deadlocks on that registry.
Findings.Headline: Early return in Registry.Disable leaves the mutex locked

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: The nil guard for `r.Ticket` no longer returns early — it falls through to `r.Ticket.Key`, which dereferences a nil `*Ticket` whenever a `Result` has no linked ticket. Since `Ticket` is documented as optional, any caller passing a `Result` with a nil `Ticket` now panics instead of rendering the body alone.
Findings.Headline: Summarize dereferences nil Ticket instead of returning Body
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Findings.Comment: Clamping the exclusive end to `len(lines) + 1` leaves `lines[first:last]` with a bound one past the slice length, so the function panics with `slice bounds out of range` on any call whose window reaches the end of the file. With `lines` of length 5, `h = {Start: 3, Count: 1}`, `n = 2`: `first` is 4, `last` is 6, the guard fires and sets `last` to 6, then `lines[4:6]` panics. Go slice bounds are exclusive, so the clamp overshoots the last line the doc comment says the window must stop at.
Findings.Headline: ContextAfter panics when the context window reaches end of file

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: Removing `defer resp.Body.Close()` from `WhoAmI` leaves the response body unclosed on every call. `Client.http.Do(req)` hands back a body whose lifetime this function owns — nothing else can close it, since only `*User` and `error` are returned. On any realistic stream of `WhoAmI` calls the idle connections are never returned to the transport's pool and the file descriptors backing them are held until process exit, so a long-running service leaks connections until it starts failing dials. The decode error path and the status-code error path leak identically to the success path.
Findings.Headline: WhoAmI no longer closes the HTTP response body

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: Removing `q.mu.Lock()` / `q.mu.Unlock()` leaves `q.depth = len(q.pending)` in `worker()` as an unsynchronized write to a field that `Submit` writes and `Depth` reads under `q.mu`. With one review submitting while the worker finishes a job, the unsynchronized write in the worker races with the `Submit` write (`q.depth = len(q.pending)`) and with `Depth`'s `return q.depth`; Go treats this as a data race with undefined behavior, and `-race` builds report it. The mutex on `Depth` and `Submit` is now protecting only part of the field's accesses, which is exactly what it existed to prevent.
Findings.Headline: Worker updates q.depth without holding the mutex

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: In an async function, `return this.refresh(base)` hands the promise straight to the caller without awaiting it inside the `try` block, so a rejected `provider.fetch` bypasses this `catch` entirely. Concretely: an expired table is cached, the provider throws, `getRates` is expected to log a warning and return `cached` — instead the rejection propagates to `getRates`'s caller and the request fails. The whole stale-serving path added here is therefore unreachable, and `staleServedCount` can never increment. `return await` is what keeps the await inside the `try`'s scope.
Findings.Headline: Stale-rate fallback never runs: return of unawaited promise skips catch

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: Dropping the error from `tx.Commit(ctx)` makes `AddClaim` report success whenever the COMMIT fails, so a claim that was never durably persisted is treated as recorded. On a realistic path (connection dropped or serialization/deadlock failure at commit time) the caller gets `nil`, the claim is absent from `team_claims`, and there is no retry or warning. The previous code returned a wrapped error here; restoring an explicit check preserves that guarantee.
Findings.Headline: Commit error silently discarded in AddClaim

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The two error returns are inverted relative to the documented contract: `errors.Is(err, errNoRows)` (the "nobody owns it" case) now wraps the raw pgx error instead of `ErrNoClaim`, while genuine database faults wrap `ErrNoClaim`. In practice a caller checking `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` before allowing a claim will fail to claim an unowned project, and conversely will treat a transient DB failure as "no owner" and claim a project that already has an owner, overwriting or racing the real owner's claim. This contradicts the comment above `Owner`: "Callers distinguish 'nobody owns it' from a database fault with errors.Is." The two branches need to wrap the values the other way round.
Findings.Headline: ErrNoClaim and raw error wrapping swapped in Owner

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
